title: Genesis 34. The Cup of Violence.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 34. The Cup of Violence.
Now Dinah, the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob,
went out to see the daughters of the land.
Dinah.
The only named daughter of Jacob.
The girl whose birth was recorded in one line at the end of chapter thirty,
and afterwards she bore a daughter and named her Dinah.
Judgment.
The daughter whose name means judgment now goes out to see.
The same verb used of God seeing creation, it was good.
The same verb used of Eve seeing the fruit, it was desirable.
Dinah goes out to see, and she is seen.
Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the land, saw her.
He took her.
He lay with her.
He violated her.
Saw.
Took.
Lay.
The same sequence as Eve in the garden, she saw, she took,
she ate.
The grabber pattern: see, take, consume.
But where Eve's taking was of fruit,
Shechem's taking is of a person.
Where the fruit was offered freely by the tree,
Dinah was taken by force from the field.
The Cup of violence begins with the same three verbs that began every other taking in Genesis,
but here the object is a daughter of the covenant.
God does not speak in this chapter.
No covenant promise.
No the Lord was with.
No divine appearance.
No dream.
No angel.
This is the only chapter in the Jacob narrative where God is silent.
The Cup of violence is a human-only cup.
The vessel that holds it has no divine light to see by.
His soul clung to Dinah, daughter of Jacob.
He loved the young woman.
He spoke to her heart.
After the violation, love.
After the taking, tenderness.
The text holds both without resolving them.
Shechem's love is real.
His violation was also real.
The cup is filled from the wrong end,
desire that took before it asked,
love that followed force instead of preceding it.
The Book of Witness does not say the love was false.
It says the violation was real.
Shechem spoke to his father Hamor:
Get me this young lady as a wife.
Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter.
His sons were with the livestock in the field.
Jacob held his peace until they came.
Jacob is silent.
The father who wrestled with God, who reconciled with Esau,
who built an altar and named it El Elohe Yisrael, says nothing.
The man who acted decisively with Esau now waits.
The man who divided his household by favoritism now withholds his voice.
His silence creates a space.
And the space will be filled.
The sons of Jacob came in from the field when they heard.
The men were grieved.
They were very angry.
Because he had done a disgraceful thing in Israel,
to lie with Jacob's daughter, and so it should not be done.
In Israel.
The first use of Israel as a collective identity.
Not the man, the people.
The covenant name given at Peniel now covers the family.
The violation is against the covenant community, not just a woman.
The name that was given in wrestling is now used in grief.
The Cup of the covenant, which was cracked at Peniel,
is now cracked again by violence against the covenant's daughter.
Hamor spoke: The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter.
Please give her to him as a wife.
Make marriages with us.
Give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves.
You shall dwell with us.
The land will be before you.
Live and trade in it.
Get possessions.
The offer of integration.
The same offer that would later threaten Israel's identity throughout the Old Testament,
assimilation through intermarriage.
Here it is offered by the aggressor's family.
The man who violated the daughter now wants to marry her.
The father of the violator offers land and trade and unity.
The Cup of the covenant is being offered a place at the table of the people who harmed it.
Shechem said: Let me find favor in your eyes.
Whatever you will tell me I will give.
Ask me never so much dowry and gift,
I will give according to what you ask.
But give me the young lady as a wife.
The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and Hamor his father with deception,
because he had defiled Dinah their sister.
Deception.
The same word used of Jacob deceiving Isaac in chapter twenty-seven.
The deception pattern transfers from father to sons.
Jacob deceived his father with goatskin.
The sons deceive their would-be father-in-law with circumcision.
The grabber's children inherit the deceiver's method.
The Cup that was held by a deceiver is now held by deceivers.
They said: We cannot do this thing,
to give our sister to a man who is uncircumcised.
That is a reproach to us.
Only on this condition will we consent:
if you will be as we are,
that every male of you be circumcised.
Then we will give our daughters to you,
and we will take your daughters for ourselves,
and we will dwell with you, and we will become one people.
Circumcision.
The covenant sign given to Abraham in chapter seventeen.
The sign that marked the flesh of every male in the covenant household.
The sign that said: this body belongs to God.
Now used as a trap.
The covenant sign becomes the instrument of murder.
The Cup of covenant is poured into the Cup of violence.
The sign of God's promise is weaponized by the promise's heirs.
Their words pleased Hamor and Shechem.
The young man did not delay to do this thing,
because he had delight in Jacob's daughter.
He was honored above all the house of his father.
Hamor and Shechem came to the gate of their city and spoke to the men:
These men are peaceful with us.
Let them live in the land and trade in it.
The land is large enough.
Let us take their daughters for wives.
Only on this condition will the men consent,
if every male among us be circumcised.
Won't their livestock and their possessions and all their animals be ours?
Only let us give our consent, and they will dwell with us.
The city agrees.
The men who violated Dinah now accept the covenant sign,
not because they believe the covenant, but because they want the wealth.
The recognition gap is absolute.
The brothers see enemies.
The city sees neighbors and profit.
The men of Shechem do not recognize the brothers as killers.
They recognize them as trading partners.
All who went out of the gate of his city listened to Hamor and Shechem.
Every male was circumcised.
On the third day, when they were sore, two of Jacob's sons,
Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, each took his sword.
They came upon the unsuspecting city.
They killed every male.
The third day.
In Genesis, the third day has been a day of arrival,
Abraham saw the place on the third day.
But here the third day is the day of greatest vulnerability.
The men of Shechem are healing from circumcision.
They are in pain.
They are defenseless.
And two brothers walk in with swords.
The Cup of violence overflows.
What began as one man's violation of one woman becomes two brothers killing every male in a city.
The revenge is disproportionate.
The city trusted them.
The men accepted the covenant sign.
And on the third day, the day of healing,
Simeon and Levi came upon the city in safety.
in trust.
In confidence.
The city was at peace.
The brothers were at war.
They killed Hamor and Shechem with the sword.
They took Dinah from Shechem's house.
They went out.
The sons of Jacob came upon the slain and plundered the city,
because they had defiled their sister.
They took their flocks, their herds, their donkeys,
that which was in the city,
and that which was in the field.
All their wealth.
All their little ones.
Their wives.
Everything in the houses.
The slaughter spreads.
Simeon and Levi killed.
The other brothers plundered.
The violence cascades from murder to looting to captivity.
The Cup that was filled with righteous anger overflows into greed.
The brothers who were grieved because a disgraceful thing was done in Israel now do a disgraceful thing themselves,
they take women and children as plunder.
The men who were angry about their sister being treated as an object now treat other women as objects.
Jacob said to Simeon and Levi: You have brought trouble on me,
making me odious among the inhabitants of the land,
the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
I am few in number.
They will gather against me, and I will be destroyed,
I and my house.
Jacob's response is fear.
Not moral outrage.
Not: you murdered innocent men.
Not: you used the covenant sign as a weapon.
Not: you took women and children as plunder.
His response is: you have made me odious.
I will be destroyed.
The father who was silent when his daughter was violated now speaks,
not about the violation, but about the consequence.
His recognition is strategic, not moral.
He sees the danger to himself.
He does not see his own silence as part of what created the violence.
They said: Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?
The chapter ends on a question.
No resolution.
No divine response.
No covenant word.
No altar.
The last word is the brothers' defense of their violence.
Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?
The question exposes the wound.
Dinah was treated as an object.
The brothers' violence was also the treatment of a city as an object.
The same pattern, seeing and taking,
that began with Shechem seeing Dinah continued with the brothers seeing the city.
The Cup of violence reproduces itself.
The grabber pattern, see, take, consume,
runs from Shechem to Simeon to Levi to the other brothers.
Everyone takes.
No one asks.
The Cup of violence is the only chapter in Genesis where God does not speak.
The promise is silent.
The covenant is absent.
The altar that was built at Shechem in chapter thirty-three,
El Elohe Yisrael,
stands in the same city where the sons of Israel committed slaughter.
The altar and the blood are in the same field.
The name Israel, given at Peniel, proclaimed at Shechem,
is now attached to a massacre.
The Cup holds.
But the vessel is stained.
The silence of the father produced the violence of the sons.
The deception of the father became the deception of the children.
The covenant sign was weaponized.
The land that was bought for a hundred pieces of money is now soaked with the blood of the men who agreed to receive that covenant sign.
The field of the promise is watered by the wrong rain.
God is silent in this chapter.
But the silence does not last.
The next chapter will break it.
The Cup that was violated, by Shechem, by Simeon, by Levi,
by Jacob's silence, will be spoken to again.
God will speak.
The silence of chapter thirty-four will end.
But the stain will remain.
The name Israel will carry what happened at Shechem until Jacob speaks his final words in chapter forty-nine:
Simeon and Levi are brothers.
Weapons of violence are their swords.
Let my soul not come into their council.
Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce.
And their wrath, for it is cruel.
The Cup of violence is not the Cup of the covenant.
But the covenant's sons held it.
And the stain does not wash out.
